title: The Last Name Is Mother
hookLine: the hymn's last names: Shiva and Shakti as one form, and then simply the mother, Lalitambika
carry: shiva and shakti are one, and she is mother

lines: A BEAD WHERE THE ENDS MEET.
cards: Some strings of prayer beads have a larger bead where the two ends meet. Move bead by bead and the fingers come back to it: the end of the round is where it started. The Lalita Sahasranama has a shape a little like that.

It opens by calling the goddess Sri Mata, the auspicious mother. And after everything in between, the hands, the war, the five acts, the climb through the body, the names of without, it closes on the mother again.

teach.b: The final names, in paraphrase. Sri Shiva: the auspicious one, given the very name of Shiva.

teach.h: ONE FORM OF SHIVA AND SHAKTI.
teach.b: Then: the one whose form is the oneness of Shiva and Shakti. And last: Lalitambika, Lalita the mother. Take the middle one first.
Shiva and Shakti can sound like two gods, a husband and a wife. This name says something bigger, and it's a core teaching of the goddess's devotees: Shiva and Shakti are one reality.
Shiva is its stillness, pure awareness; Shakti is its power, everything that moves. You can't have one without the other, and this name says that single form is hers.

teach.h: JOINED LIKE A WORD AND ITS MEANING.
teach.b: The poet Kalidasa, opening one of his poems, pictures the divine couple joined like a word and its meaning. Nobody can hold the meaning in one hand and the word in the other.
It's the same idea people see in Ardhanarishvara, the image that's half Shiva, half Parvati, in one body. Then the very last name.
Tradition hears play in the name Lalita, and amba is mother.
After a noose and a goad, a war, Kama brought back from ash, a power rising through the spine, and names that say no form can hold her, the last word isn't a throne or a weapon. It's mother.
That's the second teaching, and Hindus live it every day: the highest reality can be called Ma.
Some devotees hear a homecoming in that ending; others hear the oneness in the name before it: the mother is the whole of reality, playing.

how: In recitation of the Lalita Sahasranama the closing names, Sri Shiva, Shivashaktyaikyarupini and Lalitambika, end the hymn, and in a name-by-name archana the last offering is made with the name Lalitambika.

o: a hymn whose last name is the warrior queen
a hymn that ends on Shiva alone, not the goddess
a hymn of names that opens and closes on the mother

games.q: the last names: tap the pairs.
p: the auspicious mother: how it opens
given the very name of Shiva
one form, and it is hers
Lalita the mother: how it closes

s: the hymn ends on a name for her throne
it ends on Lalitambika, Lalita the mother.
just before the last name, the hymn names her as the oneness of Shiva and Shakti
in the goddess's devotion, Shiva and Shakti are two separate gods who only work together
the hymn names her their one form: stillness and power, one reality.

games.q: you're choosing the very last word for a hymn that has praised the goddess as queen, warrior, creator, and the formless. what does the Lalita Sahasranama choose?
o: a name for her victory in war.
games.why: after the oneness of Shiva and Shakti, the hymn ends on Lalitambika, and comes round to the mother it began with.

practice: Notice the turn at the top and the bottom of each breath: each one ends where the next begins, like beads on a string. Near the end, bring to mind someone who has looked after you, and let the breath come round to them.
If you pray, you can say the name Lalitambika, or the name you use for the one who holds you, once, quietly; if you don't, let the breath be the bead.

wordCard.voice: The Lalita Sahasranama. A hymn that opens with the auspicious mother and closes with Lalitambika, Lalita the mother.

orig.note: Sanskrit lalitāmbikā: Lalita, and ambikā, mother. the hymn's last name.

carryVoice: Your line: Shiva and Shakti are one, and she is mother. The string comes round to where it began. Rest well.
